title: Tail Codes: How One Receptor Branches and Ends Signaling

scenes.visual: Dark slate frame continuing the first film's world and colour map: the activated teal receptor pair in a grey plasma membrane, its bright gold kinases hanging over long flexible tails. Bold white title 'Tail Codes: How One Receptor Branches and Ends Signaling' fades cleanly at 2 seconds. Small 'Schematic' tag in corner.

scenes.tts: In the first film, bringing two receptor kinases together released their brake and activated the pair. Yet one active receptor starts several pathways at once and also schedules its own shutoff. How can phosphotyrosines on one receptor pick different partners and end signaling?

scenes.visual: Camera glides smoothly down the same active teal/gold receptor pair so the two long flexible cytoplasmic tails fill 65% of the frame height. Unlabelled tyrosines ('Y') sit spaced along the tails while faint outlines of multiple downstream paths pulse below.
scenes.narration: In the first film, bringing two receptor kinases together released their brake and activated the pair. Yet one active receptor starts several pathways at once and also schedules its own shutoff. How can phosphotyrosines on one receptor pick different partners and end signaling?

scenes.tts: Once switched on, the paired kinases add phosphates to tyrosines outside the catalytic core. In the epidermal growth factor receptor, most of those tyrosines sit along its flexible tails. Each newly phosphorylated tyrosine turns into a docking site for proteins floating in the cytosol.

scenes.visual: The glowing gold kinases sweep bright yellow phosphate circles ('P') onto spaced tyrosines along both tails, turning them into glowing yellow docking badges ('pY'). Softly drifting cytosolic proteins begin moving upward toward the phosphorylated tails.
scenes.narration: Once switched on, the paired kinases add phosphates to tyrosines outside the catalytic core. scenes.tts: Inside the cell, signaling proteins read those marks with pockets called S H two domains. Such a pocket does not grab just any phosphotyrosine. It grips the phosphate and checks the few amino acids right after it. Mismatched proteins bounce away, while matching partners lock on.
scenes.caption: Inside the cell, signaling proteins read those marks with pockets called SH2 domains. Such a pocket does not grab just any phosphotyrosine. It grips the phosphate and checks the few amino acids right after it. Mismatched proteins bounce away, while matching partners lock on.
scenes.visual: Zoom closer on two glowing yellow phosphotyrosine badges, each revealing a short sequence tab right beside the phosphate ('+2 Asn' in emerald accent, '+3 Met' in magenta accent; labelled 'Schematic'). An emerald SH2 block drifts toward the magenta tab, fails to fit, and bounces off gently; it then glides to the emerald '+2 Asn' tab and snaps firmly into place.
scenes.narration: Inside the cell, signaling proteins read those marks with pockets called SH2 domains. Such a pocket does not grab just any phosphotyrosine. It grips the phosphate and checks the few amino acids right after it. Mismatched proteins bounce away, while matching partners lock on.

scenes.tts: Watch how that local sequence splits one receptor into several pathways. One phosphotyrosine on the epidermal growth factor receptor tail carries an asparagine two residues later. That suits the adaptor Grb two, launching Ras and MAP kinase. Another site recruits PLC gamma, an enzyme that splits a membrane lipid into two messengers.

scenes.visual: Pull back to show both phosphorylated tails. The emerald block labelled 'Grb2' snaps onto its '+2 Asn' site (on-screen badge 'pY1068'), lighting a crisp emerald arrow down to 'Ras → MAP kinase'. Simultaneously, a sky-blue block labelled 'PLC-gamma' snaps onto a second site ('pY992'), lighting a sky-blue arrow down to 'IP3 + DAG'. Empathy fix: As PLC-gamma docks, show 'PIP2 → IP3 + DAG' beside it.

scenes.tts: Swapping the receptor partner shifts the pathway mix. Remember violet Her three from the first film. Its tail carries six tyrosines, each followed three residues later by methionine. Paired with Her two, those sites recruit PI three kinase, which drives the Akt growth and survival branch.
scenes.caption: Swapping the receptor partner shifts the pathway mix. Remember violet HER3 from the first film. Its tail carries six tyrosines, each followed three residues later by methionine. Paired with HER2, those sites recruit PI 3-kinase, which drives the Akt growth and survival branch.
scenes.visual: Swap the left teal receptor smoothly for the exact violet 'HER3' receptor from the first film, paired with teal/gold 'HER2'. Six yellow phosphotyrosines with magenta '+3 Met' tabs light up along HER3's tail (on-screen badge '6 × YXXM'). Multiple magenta 'PI 3-kinase' blocks dock along the tail, thickening a bold magenta arrow down to 'Akt'. Empathy fix: Show 'PI3K → Akt (growth, survival)' as the branch is named.

scenes.tts: Not every receptor puts all its docking sites on its own tail. Some use the stretch just under the membrane, or a loop inserted inside the kinase. The insulin receptor places many sites on separate adaptor proteins instead. Yet the same kind of sequence code still selects each partner.

scenes.visual: Slide the HER2–HER3 pair aside smoothly to show an activated teal/gold insulin receptor phosphorylating a separate floating adaptor block labelled 'IRS proteins'. The same yellow 'pY' badges light up on the IRS block, recruiting matching emerald and magenta SH2 partners, before returning cleanly to the teal receptor pair. Empathy fix: Small arrows point to the two regions as spoken, labelled 'Just under membrane' and 'Kinase insert loop'.

scenes.tts: Here is the rule that organizes receptor output. Phosphotyrosines recruit specific partners by sequence to branch and end signaling. The tail even recruits its own removal tagger, the ubiquitin ligase Cbl. Pause and predict. If a mutant loses that Cbl docking site, what happens to the active receptor?

scenes.visual: Focus on the activated teal receptor pair with emerald Grb2 and sky-blue PLC-gamma docked. Highlight one distinct orange-accented phosphotyrosine site labelled 'Cbl site', then cross it out as an orange 'Cbl' block drifts nearby. A clean top banner asks: 'Lost Cbl site: what happens to the receptor?'

scenes.visual: Hold the question 'Lost Cbl site: what happens to the receptor?' on screen above the receptor pair with the crossed-out Cbl site and floating orange Cbl block, with gentle ambient drift and a slow bottom progress bar.

scenes.tts: It is removed more slowly, so it keeps signaling longer. Normally, Cbl docks there and attaches ubiquitin tags. The receptor is taken in by endocytosis, and those tags route it to the lysosome for digestion. Meanwhile, protein tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphates straight off the tail, erasing docking sites directly.

scenes.visual: Dismiss the banner. Show the mutant pair staying lit, its partners still docked, while a schematic clock runs longer; then restore the intact site: orange 'Cbl' snaps on and attaches small orange 'Ub' tags. The grey membrane pinches inward around the tagged pair, forming an endocytic vesicle that travels down to a warm-red 'Lysosome' compartment. Beside a second surface pair, silver 'PTPs' sweep across the tail and pluck yellow 'P' circles off directly, releasing docked partners.
scenes.narration: It is removed more slowly, so it keeps signaling longer. Normally, Cbl docks there and attaches ubiquitin tags. The receptor is taken in by endocytosis, and those tags route it to the lysosome for digestion. Meanwhile, protein tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphates straight off the tail, erasing docking sites directly.

scenes.tts: One active receptor pair therefore acts like a sequence-coded switchboard. Kinases write phosphate marks, and neighboring amino acids largely decide whether a growth branch or a removal tagger lands. Together, tyrosine phosphatases and lysosomal digestion clear the board until the next growth factor arrives.
